source.title: Damage to the prefrontal cortex increases utilitarian moral judgements

confidence_rationale: This is a causal (lesion) complement to the correlational fMRI evidence in this same directory (Shenhav & Greene 2010, Bartra et al. 2013). Six patients with focal bilateral damage to ventromedial prefrontal cortex -- the same region identified as the domain-general valuation hub -- showed a selectively abnormal, more utilitarian pattern of moral judgment on emotionally aversive high-conflict dilemmas, while judgments on other classes of moral dilemma were normal. This supports ARC-121's claim that harm/ethics evaluation depends on shared circuitry (here, causally, not just correlationally) rather than a separable, independently-implemented moral module -- damage to the shared valuation/emotion hub selectively disrupts a specific class of moral judgment, exactly as would be predicted if that hub is a genuine SHARED dependency rather than incidental co-activation.
failure_signatures: The authors frame VMPC as 'necessary for the normal generation of emotions, and, in particular, social emotions' -- the paper's own interpretation emphasizes VMPC's EMOTIONAL role rather than a generic VALUATION role, which leaves open a competing reading: VMPC damage could disrupt moral judgment via a specific emotional-generation deficit rather than via disruption of a shared epistemic/valuation STATE object as ARC-121 frames it. The causal mechanism (emotion vs. shared-value-state) is under-determined by this study alone.

The effect is SELECTIVE (normal judgments on other classes of moral dilemma, only abnormal on high-conflict, aggregate-welfare-vs-emotionally-aversive-behavior dilemmas) -- a caution against reading this as evidence that ALL harm/ethics evaluation routes through this one hub; it may be specifically the emotionally-loaded conflict cases that recruit it.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Six patients with focal bilateral ventromedial prefrontal cortex (VMPC) damage produce an abnormally utilitarian pattern of judgment specifically on high-conflict moral dilemmas that pit aggregate welfare against emotionally aversive behaviors (e.g. sacrificing one life to save several), while their judgments on other classes of moral dilemma remain normal -- indicating VMPC is causally necessary for normal judgment on this selective set of dilemmas.
mapping.ree_translation: Where Shenhav & Greene (2010, this directory) show CORRELATIONAL evidence that moral judgment recruits the same regions as general valuation, Koenigs et al. supply CAUSAL evidence: damaging that shared hub selectively disrupts a class of moral judgment. This strengthens ARC-121's claim that harm/ethics evaluation genuinely DEPENDS ON the shared valuation/emotion substrate rather than merely co-activating it incidentally -- a lesion to the shared resource produces the predicted selective deficit.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The paper's own framing emphasizes VMPC's role in generating EMOTIONS (especially social emotions) rather than a generic domain-general VALUE signal -- this is a related but not identical claim to ARC-121's 'shared epistemic-state object' framing, and the selective (not global) nature of the deficit means this evidence should not be over-read as showing ALL harm/ethics evaluation depends on this one shared hub.
mapping.source_context: Human clinical lesion study; six patients with focal bilateral adult-onset VMPC damage, compared against brain-damaged and normal control groups, on a battery of moral dilemma vignettes varying in emotional salience and personal-force structure.

confidence_components.notes: Classic, highly-cited causal lesion study providing a necessary complement to the correlational fMRI evidence in this pull. Mapping fidelity is moderate: the paper's own emotion-generation framing is a related-but-distinct account from ARC-121's shared-epistemic-state framing, and the selective (not global) nature of the deficit limits how far the finding generalizes.
